overview: The Qara Khitai built a Central Asian empire after Khitan leaders moved west from the collapsing Liao world. Its history runs from 1124 to the Mongol conquest in 1218, with a change of ruling dynasty in 1211. This imported map starts only in 1200 and ends in 1279; its oversized outline extends far into the northern steppe. Treat it as a rough regional marker, not an exact frontier or survival date.

periods.title: A new western state
periods.summary: Yelü Dashi began his independent career in 1124 and took an imperial title in 1131 or 1132.

periods.title: A regional imperial power
periods.summary: Victory over the Seljuks helped establish a realm that combined directly governed territory with subordinate states.

periods.title: Usurpation and Mongol conquest
periods.summary: Kuchlug displaced the last Gürkhan in 1211; the Mongols ended his rule in 1218.

items.text: Khitan refugees from the Jin conquest of Liao established the new ruling group. Their empire eventually reached from the Oxus region toward the Altai, including much of Xinjiang. Calling it Western Liao preserves its eastern dynastic connection, although its political center now lay in Central Asia.

The victory over the Seljuks in 1141 had an extraordinary afterlife: news of it helped inspire the European legend of Prester John. A real Central Asian military success became material for a distant imagined Christian ruler. The Qara Khitai rulers themselves were Buddhist.

Most subordinate rulers kept their own titles and armies. The Qara Khitai directly administered the region around their capital, Balasaghun, but generally did not station permanent troops throughout their vassal states. Governing this empire involved working through other governments.

Women could exercise supreme political authority. After Yelü Dashi died in 1143, his widow Tabuyan governed while their son was young. Later, Pusuwan, the sister of Yelü Yilie, took power when his sons were still children. These were consequential rulers making military and diplomatic decisions, not merely names beside a king.

Royal family relationships shaped politics. The Yelü ruling family maintained marriage links with the Xiao family: Tabuyan came from Xiao, and Pusuwan married Xiao Duolubu. Such connections helped organize authority and military leadership. This evidence concerns elite families; it does not describe every household in the empire.

The ruling court moved between seasonal pastures. Its route linked winter grazing around Balasaghun with summer areas near the Tian Shan and Issyk Kul. Kochkor lay on this travel corridor. For these mobile elites, changing the season could mean changing the address.

Balasaghun was an established town before the Qara Khitai arrived. Its baked-brick minaret, with a spiral staircase inside, dates to the late tenth or early eleventh century. Archaeologists have also found houses, market areas, pottery and jewelry across the town’s long occupation. The new rulers inherited a working urban landscape.

Merchants connected places on both sides of the empire. Biran’s study identifies goods from Jin and Song China at Balasaghun and Samarkand, and Muslim merchants from Balasaghun visiting Jin markets. Much eastern commerce appears to have passed through the Tangut state. A journey to market could cross several governments.

Fine robes associated with the Khitai were prized at Seljuk and Khwarazmian courts, while Qara Khitai wine reached Jin markets. These exchanges carried fashions and tastes as well as money. They also depended on travelers who could negotiate unfamiliar places and political boundaries.

At Kök-Tash in Kyrgyzstan, researchers argue that an underground, house-like brick mausoleum belonged to Qara Khitai elites. It combined features comparable to Liao tombs with local building materials. Its disturbed history makes the attribution a careful archaeological argument, rather than a name conveniently written above the door.

Fragments from that mausoleum allowed archaeologists to reconstruct a blue-glazed ceramic table only 21 centimeters high, standing on four legs. Bronze mirrors and jade plates were also found. These are glimpses of elite funerary equipment, not a shopping list for an ordinary family’s kitchen.

sections.title: Belief, learning and a written message

items.text: Buddhist rulers governed a population that was largely Muslim and settled. Their generally tolerant policies allowed different religious communities to persist under the same imperial roof. The arrangement depended heavily on local institutions and rulers, rather than making every subject adopt the court’s religion.

Learning continued in the subordinate Qarakhanid cities. In Bukhara in 1200, al-Faryabi wrote a work on morality and piety, drawing on earlier books and providing a bibliography. Even medieval authors had to keep track of their reading! This is evidence for learned book culture, not universal school attendance.

A tiny writing sample survives on coins: 續興, read Xuxing, means roughly “Continued prosperity.” It is the era-name portion of the Chinese legend 續興元寳. Numismatists attribute these coins to Yelü Yilie in the mid-twelfth century. The sample is Chinese used by the ruling state, not a translation of Khitan.

The round coins have square central holes. Examples reported from several sites in the Chu valley helped researchers correct an earlier misreading of the inscription and reconsider the emperor’s recorded era name. A small object can make historians reopen a large book, though the reported findspots are not sealed archaeological deposits.

ending.text: Kuchlug seized power in 1211; the last Khitan Gürkhan died in 1213. Mongol forces eliminated Kuchlug in 1218, ending the polity. The imported 1279 cutoff therefore does not mark its historical fall. Its people and their skills continued under new rulers.
